words: listen; take a turn; look; voice
cross_subject: ela:ek-discussion (same class talk rules and turn words)
notes: Unit 1, Hello, our class. The child learns two pictured steps for class talk, "eyes look, wait my turn", and acts them in a circle game with a talking object; checked by doing the two steps once with the teacher watching. First year: school-day talk only, one listener and one speaker.

Unit 1, Hello, our class. The child learns one way to start a friendship, "ask to play", and rehearses it with a puppet and then a partner at free play; checked by saying the ask-to-play words in a pictured case. Cases are classroom play only. First year: starting a friendship, not yet keeping one. Teacher note: no child is asked to name who their friends are, or who is not.

Unit 1, Hello, our class. The child learns the words for asking a grown-up for help ("Can you help me?") and names the school helpers by picture (teacher, office, nurse); rehearsed with a puppet stuck on a zipper or a lost crayon. First year: asking only, for small school-day needs. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 1, Hello, our class. The child notices one thing a classmate did well in a pictured story ("she shared the blocks") and says it with a frame, "I saw you ___"; practiced as a closing circle. Praise names an action, never a look or a trait. The band starts with one noticed action, said aloud.

Unit 1, Hello, our class. The child makes an "all about me" picture of things they like to do and one group they belong to (our class), using an invented character's page as the model first. First year: one group, the class, and things the child likes. Teacher note: a child may draw a made-up page; families and culture are never asked about by name, and any family shown is the child's own choice; families of every kind appear in the model pages.

cross_subject: health:k-meh-feeling-words (health uses the same feeling words for health topics)
notes: Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child names four feelings from faces in a picture book and points to the face that matches a story character, then plays a feelings-faces matching game; checked by naming a character's feeling from a picture and one clue (the face). The class keeps one feelings-faces chart all year. Where K to 2 begins: four feelings read from faces. Teacher note: feelings are named for characters; a child is never asked how they feel in a check.

Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child links one feeling to one cause in a story ("the bear is sad because the rain stopped the picnic") with the frame "___ feels ___ because ___", said aloud. First year: one cause, one feeling, a story moment only.

Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child acts out, with a puppet, a character with a big mad feeling who stops before grabbing, using the pictured step "stop" from the calm-down steps; checked by showing the stop step on a scene card. The point is that a feeling is fine and the action is chosen, not that a feeling is hidden. Where the band begins: one step, stop, between the feeling and the action.

cross_subject: health:k-meh-calm-body (health applies the same calm body routine)
notes: Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child learns two pictured calm-down steps, "stop, breathe" (a slow balloon breath), and rehearses them as a body routine at the start of each session; checked by doing both steps when the teacher shows the card. First year: two body steps, done with the teacher. Teacher note: a plain body skill with no religious or spiritual framing; no clinical words. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child picks one class job or choice-time activity from pictures and says "I choose ___", then tries it; the class votes with pictures on one small class choice (which song to start the day). First year: one small choice that shapes the child's own day.

Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child practices starting a small task without being asked twice (getting out a book at the start signal), rehearsed as a "ready, go" game; checked by doing the first step after one signal. First year: starting a school-day task on one signal.

words: clean up; put away; first, next
notes: Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child follows a two-picture "first, next" routine for tidying a center and putting materials away, practiced at the end of each session; checked by doing both steps from the picture card. The band opens with a two-picture routine for one place.

Unit 2, Naming my feelings. The child keeps working on one short task (a puzzle, a drawing) to the end of a sand timer with the cue "eyes on my work"; the timer is a pace cue for a short task, not a race. Checked by finishing one small task. First year: one short task finished, with one cue.

Unit 3, Being me. The child names one thing they are good at or can do (tie a shoe, sing, help a friend), first for an invented character, then for themselves if they choose, drawn on a strengths page. First year: one strength, named for a character before oneself. Teacher note: strengths from home languages and culture are welcome when a child offers them; the course never asks about a child's culture by name.

Unit 3, Being me. The child hears a story where a character breaks a cup and chooses whether to tell; the child picks the true action from two pictures and says what it costs ("he might be in trouble, but the grown-up can help"). Checked on the invented case only, never on a child's own conduct. The band starts with a choice between two pictures.

Unit 3, Being me. The child learns the words "I can try" for a hard thing and acts out a character who tries a new climb on the playground; checked by naming one step the character can take and one person to ask for help. The course never records a child's own answer. First year: three words and one step for a hard thing.

Unit 3, Being me. The child sees a character who could not hop on one foot, practiced, got help, and then could; the class tries a short new skill (a clapping pattern) three times and sees it get easier. Taught as practice and help making you better, never as a promise that believing raises results. Where K to 2 starts: a skill seen getting easier over three tries.

Unit 3, Being me. The child picks pictures of things they like to learn about and keeps them on a private "I like" page; the step checked is that the child chose and drew, never what is on the page. First year: interests picked from pictures. Teacher note: the page stays with the child.

Unit 4, Kind hearts. The child says what a story character sees or wants that is different from another character (the one who wants the swing too), with the frame "___ wants ___". First year: one other person's want, in a story moment.

Unit 4, Kind hearts. The child notices a character who is hurt or sad (fell down, lost a toy) and acts one kind action with a puppet: ask "are you OK?", get a grown-up. Checked by naming one caring action for a pictured case. The band begins with one caring action for a hurt that can be seen.

Unit 4, Kind hearts. The child reads a feeling from face and body clues in photos of invented children and the feelings-faces chart, and names the clue; played as "what is the clue?" Checked by one face, one feeling, one clue. First year: clues from the face and body only.

Unit 4, Kind hearts. The child says thank you for one thing a helper did with the frame "Thank you for ___", and the class makes a thank-you picture for a school helper. Thanks name an action, never a gift or what a family can afford. First year: thanks for one action, said with a frame.

Unit 4, Kind hearts. The child hears a story where a character guesses a new child "can't play tag" and is wrong, and learns the check "ask, don't guess"; checked by choosing the asking action on a picture card. First year: one check on one guess, in fairness at play. Teacher note: taught as checking one's own guess on invented cases, never as blame of a group.

cross_subject: social-studies:ssk-rules-why (social studies teaches why groups make rules, SEL how I act with them)
notes: Unit 4, Kind hearts. The child connects one class rule to what it helps people do ("walking feet so nobody falls") by acting the rule and its reason; the class rule poster is the case. First year: why our class has rules, nothing wider.

Unit 5, Playing together. The child learns a game from another place, taught by the teacher or a story, and plays it with a partner, saying one way people play differently and one way they are the same. First year: one way different and one the same, met through a game. Teacher note: no child is asked to teach or explain their own culture; offering is the child's choice.

Unit 5, Playing together. The child builds a block tower with a partner using one step, "take turns", from the talk turn card; checked by taking turns for one build. First year: one step, taking turns, in school-day play.

Unit 5, Playing together. Two puppets both want the same ball; the child shows two steps, "stop, breathe" then "say what you want", and the class picks a fair end (take turns, swap, share). Checked by doing both steps on a scene card. The teacher plays the puppet who is upset. The band starts with two steps and a fair end the class picks.

cross_subject: health:k-s-trusted-helpers (health names the trusted grown-ups the child walks to)
notes: Unit 5, Playing together. The child learns to say "No, I don't want to" and walk to a grown-up when a puppet (played by the teacher) asks them to do something unsafe on the playground (climb the fence). First year: one refusal sentence and a walk to a grown-up. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; no child plays the one who pressures. Health owns body safety.

Unit 5, Playing together. The child takes a turn as line leader and as follower in a "follow the leader" movement game, naming one thing a good leader does (goes slow, looks back) and one a good follower does (watches). The band begins with leading and following in a movement game.

Unit 5, Playing together. A puppet (played by the teacher) is left out of a game; the child learns two steps, "stand with them, tell a grown-up", and acts them with a card; checked on a pictured case. First year: two steps, with the grown-up doing the rest. Teacher note: no student plays the one who is unkind or the one left out; the teacher or a card does.

Unit 5, Playing together. The child hears a story where a game rule ("only kids with red shirts") leaves someone out, says why it is not fair, and the class makes an "everyone can join" rule for one center. First year: playground fairness only. Teacher note: no history or current dispute at this grade.

Unit 5, Playing together. The child sorts pictures of places (library, playground, lunch) by what they ask of us (quiet voice, running feet, waiting), and acts the right voice for a place the teacher names. First year: three school places and what each asks.

Unit 6, Good choices. The child asks one "I wonder" question about a story problem and hears a classmate's different idea, saying "that is a new idea". Practiced in a wonder circle; checked by asking one question about a pictured case. Where K to 2 begins: one wonder question about a story.

cross_subject: math:mk-sort-count (sorting and counting a class tally)
notes: Unit 6, Good choices. The class picks a class game by counting picture votes, and the child says "we checked, more chose ___"; checked by reading which group is bigger on a sorted tally. First year: counting small groups only.

Unit 6, Good choices. The child names one fix for a small class problem in a story (spilled paint, not enough glue) and acts it; one problem, one fix, at school. First year: a fix the child can act alone.

Unit 6, Good choices. The child learns the three pictured words "stop, think, choose" and says what might happen next in a picture case ("if he runs with scissors, then ___"); checked by naming one next thing for one choice. The class keeps the stop-think-choose card all year. Where the band begins: one step ahead, what happens next.

Unit 6, Good choices. The child sees two characters, one who rushes a puzzle and one who stops to think, and says which went better and why, at play and at a classroom task. First year: two characters compared, at play and at a task.

words: good for me; good for you; healthy
notes: Unit 6, Good choices. The child sorts picture choices (wash hands, share snack, push in line) into "good for me and you" or "not", and says one reason. Health owns the health topics; SEL uses everyday class choices. The band starts with a sort into two piles and one reason.

Unit 6, Good choices. The child names who a choice touches in a story (the character, a friend, the class) by placing pictures on a "who does it touch?" circle. First year: who a story choice touches, placed by picture.

Unit 6, Good choices. The child picks one small class goal from pictures (clean up the reading corner by the song's end) and one step to reach it, shown on a two-rung goal steps card, then the class tries it. Checked by naming the goal and the step. First year: one class goal and one step.

cross_subject: ela:e1-discussion (same class talk rules)
notes: Unit 1, Our class team. The child adds a step to class talk: listen, then reply on the same topic ("I agree with ___ because"), rehearsed in pairs with the talk turn card. Step up from K: a second person speaks back, so the child listens for what the other said.

Unit 1, Our class team. Small groups build a paper bridge with a job each (holder, taper, checker), using the talk turn card to share ideas; the child names their job and does it. Step up: each teammate has a different view of the task.

Unit 1, Our class team. The child notices what a teammate did well during the group task and tells them with "You were good at ___ when ___". Step up: noticing a real classmate's action in a planned task, not only a story.

Unit 1, Our class team. The child names one strength they bring to the team (counting, drawing, being calm), first for an invented teammate in a story, and places it on a team strengths poster if they choose. Step up: a strength seen through what a teammate needs. Teacher note: home languages and culture welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 2, Calm body, calm mind. The child adds four feeling words to the feelings faces chart and names a character's feeling with two clues (face and what happened). Step up: two characters in one scene can feel different things. Teacher note: feelings are named for characters in checks.

Unit 2, Calm body, calm mind. The child acts a character with a big frustrated feeling who uses "stop, breathe" and then picks what to do, and hears how the other character in the scene felt. Checked on a scene card. Step up: the choice now also looks at the other person.

Unit 2, Calm body, calm mind. The child adds count to five to the calm-down steps (the shared calm-down card, docs/courses/sel/STANDARD.md section 7) and chooses breathe or count; rehearsed every session. Step up: a partner reminds with the cue word and the child chooses the tool. Teacher note: body skill only, no spiritual framing, no clinical words. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

words: keep going; distracted; back to work
notes: Unit 2, Calm body, calm mind. The child practices getting back to work when a partner is chatting, with the cue "back to my work" said politely; checked by doing it once in a planned work time. Step up: a second person is the distraction.

Unit 2, Calm body, calm mind. The class chooses one calm corner tool for the room by a picture vote, and the child says why it helps others too. Step up: the choice shapes the group, not only the child.

Unit 2, Calm body, calm mind. The child follows two pictured steps to get ready for a task (desk clear, tools out), then starts, and checks each step on the goal steps card. Step up: the plan gets ready for a task, not only tidies after one, and is shared with a partner.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss1-community-problems (social studies looks at community problems, SEL at the child's own)
notes: Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. The child places invented problems on a three-step problem size meter (small: fix it myself; medium: ask a friend; big: get a grown-up) and names one fix for a small one. Step up from K: the fix depends on who else is in the problem.
Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. The child uses stop-think-choose on a scene card and names what happens next for the character and for one other person. Step up: two people's results.

model_in: talk turn card; problem size meter
model_out: talk turn card; problem size meter; I-statement frame
words: I feel; when; I need; disagree
notes: Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. The child learns the frame "I feel ___ when ___. I need ___." (the same three parts as health kindergarten's I-statement, docs/courses/sel/STANDARD.md section 7) and uses it with a partner on an invented disagreement (both want the same seat), after checking the problem size; the class names a fair end. Step up: the other person answers. The teacher plays any upset part.

cross_subject: health:g1-s-choose-and-ask (health applies choosing and asking to safety topics)
notes: Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. The child rehearses "No, I don't want to, let's ___ instead", then moving away and telling (the words of health grade 1's "say stop, move away, tell"), when a card character urges a rule break (taking another child's snack). Step up: offering a second idea. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; health owns body safety and medicine topics.

cross_subject: health:g1-s-ask-for-help (health applies asking for help to safety)
notes: Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. The child matches the problem size meter to who to ask (myself, a friend, a grown-up) and also practices offering help ("Do you want help?") to a puppet. Step up: help goes both ways. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. The child notices a small class problem nobody is fixing (crayons on the floor) and starts the fix without being asked, in a planned clean-up moment. Step up: noticing what others need.

Unit 3, Small problems, big problems. In a small group puzzle, the child takes a turn as leader who asks "what do you think?" and as follower who shares one idea. Step up: the leader listens to a second person's idea.

Unit 4, How do they feel? The child tells a short story from a second character's side (the wolf's or the friend's), with the frame "If I were ___, I would think ___". Step up: a full second point of view, not only what they want.

Unit 4, How do they feel? The child picks a caring action that fits what a struggling character wants (some want a friend, some want space) and acts it with a puppet. Step up: ask what the other person wants.
Unit 4, How do they feel? The child reads a feeling from voice and body as well as face in short teacher-acted scenes and names two clues. Step up: two people in the scene, two feelings.
Unit 4, How do they feel? The child writes or draws a thank-you note to a classmate naming the act and how it helped. Step up: thanks say how the act helped the other person.

Unit 4, How do they feel? The child traces how a character's feeling changed what they thought and did ("he felt left out, thought nobody liked him, so he went home"), on a three-box strip. Step up from K: the chain reaches an action.

Unit 4, How do they feel? The child spots a character's wrong guess about another child (from how they look or talk) and uses "ask, don't guess" to fix it on a scene card. Step up: the other child's side of the story is told. Teacher note: invented cases only, never blame of a group.

Unit 4, How do they feel? The child rehearses two steps when a card character is unkind to another: stand with them and say "That's not kind", then tell a grown-up. Step up: the child now speaks to the unkind act, not only stands with the one left out. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the unkind part; no student plays victim or the one who is unkind.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss1-group-rules (social studies on why groups have rules)
notes: Unit 4, How do they feel? The child finds signs and rules on a school walk (stop sign at the crossing, quiet sign at the library) and says how each shapes what people do. Step up: rules beyond the classroom, in the whole school.

Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child makes a "my circles" page of groups they belong to (class, team, club, family) from an invented character's model first. Step up: the same person belongs to many groups. Teacher note: a child may make up their page; families of every kind appear in the models; a family or culture is never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child chooses the true action in a story where telling the truth upsets a friend, and says what it costs. Step up: the truth involves a second person's feelings. Checked on the invented case only.

Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child learns two steps to keep a friendship after a small hurt, "say sorry, make it right", and rehearses them with a partner on a scene card. Step up: keeping, not only starting, a friendship. Teacher note: no child names their friends or who is not.

Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child hears a story of two friends from different places sharing foods or games, and says one thing each learned from the other, then plays a game from the story. Step up: learning from the other person, not only noticing a difference. Teacher note: no child is asked to explain their own culture.

words: fair; leave out; change the rule
notes: Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child hears a story where a club rule leaves a newcomer out, says who it leaves out and why that is unfair, and suggests a fairer rule. Step up: the newcomer's side is told. Fairness at play, no history or current dispute.

Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child compares what two invented places ask (a visit to the library, the school bus) and acts the fitting way to greet and behave in each. Step up: places outside the classroom.

Unit 5, Families, friends and me. The child asks a partner how they would build the class tower differently and says one new idea it gave them. Step up: questions to another person, not only about a story.

Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child plans two steps on the goal steps card for a character facing a hard task and one place to ask for help; the class then tries a hard challenge (a tricky tower) with those steps. The course never records a child's own answer. Step up: help comes from another person.

Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child keeps a practice chart of one skill tried over a week (a jump-rope count, writing a letter shape) and sees it grow with practice and a classmate's tip. Practice and help, never belief alone. Step up: help from a peer.

Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child adds to a private "I like" page one thing they want to learn and why; checked only that the steps were followed. Teacher note: the page stays with the child. Step up: a reason, sometimes "so I can help someone".

cross_subject: health:g1-phw-name-a-goal (health applies goals to health habits)
notes: Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child sets a two-step class goal with a partner on the goal steps card and checks it after a week. Step up: a shared goal.

cross_subject: math:m1-data-three-categories (a three-category class tally)
notes: Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The class picks how to help the school (pick up litter, read to K) from a three-choice tally and the child says what the counts show. Step up: three choices and what others prefer.

Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child uses stop-think-choose before a class helping task and says how thinking first helped the group, at school and at home. Step up: the reason is said for a group task, and home joins school.

words: good for me; good for others
notes: Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child picks a helping choice that is good for themselves and for someone else and says both reasons. Step up: two people's well-being.
Unit 6, I can try, I can help. The child names who a class helping choice touches (us, the K class, the custodian) on the "who does it touch?" circle. Step up: people outside the class.

Unit 1, Rules here and there. The child compares a fair and an unfair game rule in two invented clubs, says who each leaves out and what it costs them, and the class rewrites the unfair one. Owner year for K to 2: fairness of rules at play, with a cost named. Teacher note: playground and club fairness only; unfair rules of the past wait for grade 5 by the grade table; no current dispute.

Unit 1, Rules here and there. The child reads what an invented situation asks (a quiet test, a noisy assembly, a new classmate's first day) and the chance it offers (a new classmate's first day is a chance to be the first to say hello), acts the fitting response and names the cost of getting it wrong. Owner year for K to 2: both halves of the code, what a situation asks and the chance it offers.

Unit 1, Rules here and there. The child sorts rules of the class, school and town (crossing guard, library card) and says how each shapes what people do and what goes wrong without it. Owner year for K to 2: rules at school and in town, with a cost.

cross_subject: ela:e2-discussion (same class talk rules)
notes: Unit 1, Rules here and there. The child asks a question, then adds to a partner's idea in a planned talk about class rules, with the talk turn card; checked by doing the two steps in one talk. Listening stays the K card's step, said by the teacher as a prompt. Owner year: talk when the other person disagrees.

Unit 1, Rules here and there. The child chooses the true action in a case where a rule broken by a friend could be hidden, and says what telling costs and why it matters. Owner year for K to 2: truth with a cost. Checked on the invented case only; never on a child's own conduct.

Unit 1, Rules here and there. The child makes a thank-you card for a school or town helper named in the rules unit, saying what they did and how it helps many people. Owner year: thanks to people outside the class.

Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The child names harder feelings on the feelings faces chart and tells which clue shows a character's feeling when the face hides it. Owner year for K to 2: mixed or hidden feelings. Teacher note: feelings are named for characters in checks; no clinical words.

Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The child shows on a three-box strip how changing a thought changes a character's feeling and action ("maybe she didn't see me" turns mad into okay), with what the character cares about (being included) shown as part of the chain; an unseen item links that value to the thought and the feeling. Owner year: the chain can be changed, and values are part of it.

cross_subject: ela:e2-character-response (how story characters respond to a hard event, the cases SEL acts out)
notes: Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The child acts a character with a strong feeling under a pressure (losing a game in front of friends), uses the calm-down steps and chooses an action, then says what the other choice would have cost. Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The child chooses which calm-down tool on the shared card fits which moment (the balloon breath before a test, count to five after a bump, a stretch or asking for a break when the feeling stays big) and rehearses a two-step plan. Owner year: choosing the tool. Teacher note: body skill only, no spiritual framing; health owns mental health topics. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The child keeps working through the hard part of a task with a self-talk cue ("one more try"), in a planned work time, and says what quitting would cost. Owner year for K to 2. Also carries AASL.V.D.1 (trying again when a task gets hard), placed in SEL by library (docs/courses/library/STANDARD.md section 4); it moves into the standard cell once scripts/progression.py accepts AASL ids for SEL.

Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The child shows how an invented character feels different in different groups (proud at the team, shy at a new club) and makes their own circles page if they choose. Owner year for K to 2. Teacher note: a child may make up the page; family and culture are never asked about by name.

Unit 2, Strong feelings, steady me. The class proposes one change that would make the room calmer for everyone (a quiet signal) and tries it for a week; the child gives one reason and one cost. Owner year: student voice in class life.

Unit 3, Being a good friend. The child sorts invented friend actions into "good for a friendship" and "hurts it", and rehearses fixing one hurt. Owner year for K to 2: keeping a friendship when it costs something (sharing a turn). Teacher note: no naming of real friends.

words: I feel; when; I need; fair
notes: Unit 3, Being a good friend. Both partners use the full I-statement, "I feel ___ when ___. I need ___.", on an invented disagreement, each asks the other "What do you need?", and they agree a fair end; checked as a rehearsal against the look-fors. Owner year: the ask part (asking what the other needs), and an end both can live with. The teacher plays any upset part.

Unit 3, Being a good friend. The child decides when a friend's problem is too big for kids (problem size meter) and rehearses getting a grown-up, and offers help on a small one. Owner year for K to 2. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

cross_subject: ela:e2-points-of-view (characters who see one event differently, the same move as telling a quarrel from both sides)
notes: Unit 3, Being a good friend. The child tells a friend quarrel from both sides and says what each wants and what it costs them to give in. Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 3, Being a good friend. The child reads clues that a friend is upset when they say "I'm fine" and practices a check-in question. Owner year: hidden feelings. Teacher note: if a child tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.
Unit 3, Being a good friend. In a group game, the child leads by giving everyone a turn and follows another leader's plan even when it was not their idea. Owner year for K to 2: following has a cost.

cross_subject: health:g2-v-my-limits-say-stop (health applies refusal to body safety)
notes: Unit 4, Standing up, speaking up. The child rehearses two refusal steps, "say no with a reason, then offer something else", when a card character urges a dare or rule break; under the second push the child says it again, moves away and tells, the same words as health grade 2's boundary steps (docs/courses/sel/STANDARD.md section 7). Owner year: holding the no under a second push. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; health owns substance and body-safety topics.

Unit 4, Standing up, speaking up. The child rehearses speaking up for a card character left out or teased ("Stop, that's not fair"), standing with them and getting help, and says the cost of staying quiet. Owner year for K to 2. Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, no cause chosen by the course.

Unit 4, Standing up, speaking up. The child chooses and acts a caring follow-up for a character who was teased (sit with them, invite them in), knowing it may cost them a turn with other friends. Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 4, Standing up, speaking up. The child catches a character's snap judgment about a newcomer, checks it by asking, and names what the wrong guess cost the newcomer. Owner year for K to 2. Teacher note: invented cases; noticing one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

Unit 4, Standing up, speaking up. The child uses stop-think-choose on a speak-up case, names the likely result of two choices for each person, and judges which was better afterward. Owner year: judging the result.

words: I can; steps; help; try again
notes: Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child plans steps and a helper for a character's hard goal and a "try again" step for a setback. Owner year for K to 2. The course never records a child's own answer.

Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child tracks one skill over two weeks with practice and help, and explains a setback as "not yet with practice"; never belief alone as the cause. Owner year for K to 2. Also carries AASL.V.D.2 (skill grows with practice and help), placed in SEL by library (docs/courses/library/STANDARD.md section 4); it moves into the standard cell once scripts/progression.py accepts AASL ids for SEL.

Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child picks one interest from their private page and names a reason to work at it. Checked only that the steps were followed. Teacher note: the page stays with the child.
Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child sets a two-step goal on the goal steps card, checks progress at the end of each week and changes a step that did not work. Owner year: adjusting the plan.
Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child makes a picture-and-word plan with times for a two-day class project and keeps materials in a labeled folder. Owner year for K to 2: time is part of the plan.
Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child proposes and starts a small helping idea for the class (a book swap shelf) and says what starting it costs (time at recess). Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child names a strength they can use toward a goal and one a teammate brings, modeled first on an invented teammate whose strength comes from speaking two languages (she helps a new classmate with a word). Owner year for K to 2: the culture and language part of the code is taught on the character. Teacher note: home languages and culture welcome when offered, never asked about.
Unit 5, Goals and growing. The child gives a classmate specific feedback on what they did well in reaching a goal, with an example. Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 6, Our class helps. The child works in a mixed group on a class helping project with an invented story partner from another place, who brings one way of sharing the work from a game or chore at home (from a named source), tries it and says what it added. Owner year for K to 2: people whose cultures differ, at playground and class scale. Teacher note: no child is asked to explain their own culture; the partner's way is one child's, never a whole culture's.

Unit 6, Our class helps. The group plans and carries out a class helping project with roles, and the child solves one team problem with the talk turn card. Owner year for K to 2: teamwork when time is short. Also carries AASL.III.D.2 (the group's learning as one's own job), placed in SEL by library (docs/courses/library/STANDARD.md section 4); it moves into the standard cell once scripts/progression.py accepts AASL ids for SEL.
Unit 6, Our class helps. The child asks questions of other classes or helpers to find what the school needs and changes their idea after hearing a new one. Owner year for K to 2.

cross_subject: math:m2-picture-bar-graphs (a picture or bar graph of class votes)
notes: Unit 6, Our class helps. The class graphs a vote on which helping project to do and the child chooses from what the graph shows, not from who talks loudest. Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 6, Our class helps. The child names a school problem the class can fix (a messy hallway), sizes it on the problem size meter and picks a solution with its cost. Owner year: problems in the wider school.
Unit 6, Our class helps. The child says how careful thinking helped the project and where rushing would have cost the class, in school and at home. Owner year for K to 2.
Unit 6, Our class helps. The child weighs a helping choice for what it does for themselves, their class and the people helped. Owner year for K to 2.

Unit 6, Our class helps. The child maps who the class project touches near (class, school) and farther (families, neighbors) on the "who does it touch?" circle, and one rule it must follow. Owner year for K to 2.

words: frustrated; embarrassed; strength of a feeling; body clue
cross_subject: health:g3-meh-feelings-say (health has students say feelings in health topics with the same words)
notes: Unit 1, Think, feel, do. The feelings faces chart gains a 1 to 5 strength scale, and the student uses a three-step routine, "spot the body clue, name it, rate it", on characters in school-day scene cards (a lost recess game, a hard spelling quiz), and says why naming a feeling first makes it easier to handle. Across the band line: grade 2 named hidden and mixed feelings; grade 3 adds how strong and a named routine. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

words: thought; feeling; action; chain; kinder thought
notes: Unit 1, Think, feel, do. The student fills a think-feel-do chain for a scene-card character (a classmate did not wave back), adds what the character values (being a good friend) and explains how that value helps account for the thought and the feeling, and then uses "catch the thought, test it, try another": writes a second thought that fits the facts and shows how the feeling and action change. Grade 2 saw that the chain can change; grade 3 has the student change it, with a reason (thoughts are guesses, and guesses can be checked). Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

Unit 1, Think, feel, do. The calm-down steps grow to four for grades 3 to 5: stop, breathe, name it, choose. The student rehearses them as a routine before acting on a big feeling in a school-day case (a teammate grabs the ball), then explains in a sentence the difference between reacting and responding. From grade 2's steps used once under a push to a routine the class names and gives a reason for.

words: breathe; stretch; count; cope; plan card
notes: Unit 1, Think, feel, do. The student builds a plan card with the four calm-down steps and a menu of three body tools (slow breaths, a stretch, counting back from ten) for two school moments (before a test, after a recess argument), rehearses it daily for a week (kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue) and says why each step helps the body. Bigger than grade 2's two-step plan: four steps, each with its reason. Teacher note: breathing, stretching and pausing as plain body skills, with no spiritual framing; mental health topics are health's. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 1, Think, feel, do. Stop-think-choose grows to four steps for grades 3 to 5: stop, list two or three choices, think what each would cause, choose and check. The student compares two invented classmates doing the same school task, one who rushed and one who used the steps, and writes one place at home where the steps would help too. The K to 2 owner year said how thinking helped one project; now two cases sit side by side.

Unit 1, Think, feel, do. The student uses stop-think-choose on a school-day choice (finish a game indoors, or go out and play with a classmate who is alone) and lists what each option does for their own well-being and for the people around them, then picks with a reason. A step past grade 2: two options weighed, not one choice explained.

Unit 2, Who I am and what I bring. The student builds an identity web for an invented character (a team, a helper role at home, a club, a language) in three steps: list the groups, say what each adds, say where each part shows. They may make their own private web. Grade 2 showed one character in two groups; grade 3 builds a whole web and says why knowing it helps. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 2, Who I am and what I bring. A strengths hunt in three steps: recall a task that went well, name the skill it used, find another place it helps. Done first for a story character, then for the student if they choose, and a language spoken counts as a strength. The new demand over grade 2: each strength is backed by an example. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 2, Who I am and what I bring. On a school-day case (a classmate's answer sheet left in view), the student uses stop-think-choose to pick the honest action, names the value behind it, and says what honesty cost the character and what it kept. Grade 2 chose truth with a cost; grade 3 ties the choice to a named value. Checked on the invented case only, never on a student's own conduct.

Unit 2, Who I am and what I bring. The student keeps a private interest log for two weeks (kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue) (what they chose to do in free time, and why), then picks one entry and names a purpose for it (to help someone, to make something). The step from grade 2: the interest comes from what they actually did, not a single pick. Teacher note: the log stays with the student; it is checked only that the steps were followed, never for its content.

Unit 2, Who I am and what I bring. After a planned partner task the student gives a three-part shout-out (what they did, how they did it, why it mattered) and rewrites a vague "good job" into a specific one. Grade 2 named what and gave an example; grade 3 adds the how and the why.

words: perspective; point of view; reason; side
cross_subject: ela:e3-point-of-view (telling one's own view apart from a character's, the same move in reading)
notes: Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. The student uses a "shoes switch" on a school-day scene card: name what each person saw, what each wants and why each acted, then retell the scene from the other side. Grade 2 told both sides of a quarrel; grade 3 asks for the reason behind each side.

Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. Three care steps, "notice, ask what would help, do it", acted with a partner on a scene card where a character struggles (a lost library book, a hard reading turn); the student explains why asking first beats guessing. Up from grade 2: asking what the other person wants is now its own step, read from the feelings faces. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

words: body language; tone of voice; clue; check in
notes: Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. The student reads three kinds of clue (face, body, voice) in short teacher-acted school scenes, rates the strength on the feelings faces scale, and checks the guess with a question. Building on grade 2's hidden feelings, the guess now has a strength and a check.

Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. The class keeps a gratitude wall for two weeks (kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue); each note names the act, the person and the difference it made, and the student says why noticing good things changes a class. Grade 2 thanked a helper once; grade 3 turns thanks into a habit kept over weeks.

Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. A three-step check on a snap judgment in a school-day case (a quiet new student called stuck-up): catch the first thought, ask what I actually know, find out before deciding, using stop-think-choose. Grade 2 caught and checked a guess; grade 3 names the steps and says why first guesses mislead. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. With a story partner from another place on a shared task, the student uses three steps: notice a different way, ask about it with respect, try it or combine it. The new piece after grade 2 is the respectful question. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-rules-rights (social studies traces a rule back to the problem it solves, SEL how the rule shapes what people do)
notes: Unit 3, Walking in their shoes. The student follows one school system (the lunch line, the bus line-up) in three steps: name the rule, say what it makes people do, say what would happen without it. Grade 2 sorted rules of class, school and town; grade 3 follows one system all the way through.

words: say back; build on; clarify; respond
cross_subject: ela:e3-discussion (the same class talk norms and words)
notes: Unit 4, When friends disagree. The talk turn card grows to four steps for grades 3 to 5: listen, say back what you heard, ask a question, add your idea. The student uses it in a planned partner talk on a friend-disagreement case and gives the reason for saying back first (the other person knows they were heard). Grade 2 asked and added; saying back and listening as a named step are new.

Unit 4, When friends disagree. The student sorts friendship actions into "builds trust" and "breaks trust", then repairs a broken-trust moment from a scene card in three steps: own it, say sorry with the I-statement frame, make a plan to fix it. The student then rehearses the repair talk, saying the sorry with the I-statement frame, while the teacher or a scene card supplies the hurt friend's words and a partner coaches with the step card. Grade 2 fixed one hurt; grade 3 adds a plan. Teacher note: no real friends are named.

Unit 4, When friends disagree. The I-statement frame grows to four parts for grades 3 to 5: I feel, when, because, I need. With a partner, the student works an invented recess disagreement through "cool, talk, choose": calm first, both say an I-statement, then pick a fair solution from at least two. Grade 2 agreed one end; grade 3 compares two. The teacher plays any upset part.

words: trusted adult; help; offer; problem size
cross_subject: health:g3-s-which-helper (health names which helper fits which safety problem)
notes: Unit 4, When friends disagree. The problem size meter gains a fourth level for grades 3 to 5 (tiny, small, medium, big), each with who to go to. The student sizes school-day problems from a card deck, rehearses asking a trusted adult about a big one in three steps (go to them, say what happened, say what you need) with a partner playing the adult, and rehearses offering help on a small one aloud, the partner now playing the classmate. Grade 2 decided when a problem is too big; grade 3 rehearses the asking itself. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 4, When friends disagree. The student reads a school situation with three questions (where am I, what does this place expect, what chance does it give me) on cases like the start of a group project or a fire drill, and acts the fitting response. Grade 2 named one chance on an invented case; grade 3 asks for it with a named question on school cases.

Unit 4, When friends disagree. In a small-group disagreement case the student leads with three steps (hear every idea with the talk turn card, sum up, help the group choose), then follows another leader's choice. Grade 2 gave everyone a turn; grade 3 leads the group to a choice.

Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. A four-step refusal, "stop and think, say no clearly, give a reason, offer something else or walk away", rehearsed when a card character urges a school-day rule break (copying homework, sneaking into the closed gym); the student says why a reason makes a no stronger. Grade 2 held a no under a second push; grade 3 adds thinking before answering. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; no student plays the one who pushes; substance and body-safety topics are health's.

cross_subject: health:g3-v-bullying (health teaches what bullying is, SEL rehearses the upstander steps)
notes: Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. The student learns an upstander plan with four options (speak up with an I-statement, stand with the one left out, get help, check in after) and picks which fits each of two school cases of teasing or exclusion, with a reason. The student then rehearses the chosen words with a partner, using the I-statement frame, while the teacher or a card plays the unkind act. Up from grade 2: choosing among options. Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, and no cause is chosen by the course.

Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. Before a class choice the student asks three kinds of question (what, why, what if) of a scene-card case and changes their first idea when a new fact comes in, saying what changed their mind. Grade 2 asked and changed an idea; grade 3 names the kinds of question.

cross_subject: math:m3-scaled-graphs (reading a scaled bar graph of class data)
notes: Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. The class makes a scaled bar graph of a survey (which game for indoor recess) and the student chooses from it, saying which fact decided and which opinion did not. Grade 2 read a picture graph; grade 3 reads a scaled one and pulls fact apart from opinion.

Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. The student solves a classroom problem (crowded coat hooks) in four steps: size it, list ideas, choose one, test it for a week and check (the test kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue). The grade 2 owner row picked a solution; grade 3 tests it.

Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. On a school-day choice card the student uses stop-think-choose to predict what each of two choices causes next, later that day and next week, and judges the result after. Grade 2 judged one result; grade 3 looks along time.

Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. The student checks an invented game or club rule (only kids who own a ball may play) with three fairness questions (who can join, who is left out, how could it change) and rewrites it. Grade 2 rewrote one unfair rule; grade 3 has a named check to use on any rule. Teacher note: rules in a class, club or game on invented cases; unfair rules of the past wait for grade 5 by the grade table; no current dispute.

Unit 5, Saying no, choosing well. The student places who a class choice affects on a three-ring "who does it touch?" circle (me, my class, the school), with a reason for each, and names one school rule the choice must follow. Grade 2 named near and far; grade 3 places each person with a reason.

Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. The student plans a stretch goal for an invented character on the goal steps card (goal, steps, a likely block, a helper) and writes an "if this happens, then I will" plan for the block. Grade 2 planned a try-again step after a setback; grade 3 names the block before it happens. The course never records a student's own answer.

Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. The student keeps a three-week practice record (kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue) of one school skill (multiplication facts, a cartwheel), notes which practice or help made the biggest change, and explains growth as practice, strategy and help, never belief alone. Over grade 2: comparing which kind of practice helped most.

Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. A three-step focus plan (spot the distraction, say the cue, move seats or ask) used in a planned work time and checked off on the goal steps card, with a try-again step for when the work itself gets hard (try another way, then ask). Grade 2 used one self-talk cue; grade 3 plans for the distraction ahead of time.

cross_subject: health:g3-phw-set-goal (health applies goal setting to a health habit)
notes: Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. The goal steps card grows to four steps for grades 3 to 5: goal, steps, block and plan, check. The student sets a three-week school goal (finish a chapter book), checks weekly and changes one step; the goal is kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue. The new demand over grade 2: a block is planned for before it comes.

Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. The student plans a one-week class project on a planner with days and times, keeps a materials checklist, and reviews at the end what went to plan. Grade 2 planned two days; grade 3 a week.

Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. The student notices a class need, plans the first step on the goal steps card and starts it without being asked (a welcome kit for new students). Grade 2 started a small idea; grade 3 plans before starting.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-taking-part (social studies on how people take part in a democracy, SEL on the student's own voice in class)
notes: Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. The class proposes and votes on one change to a class routine; the student gives a reason with evidence and helps carry it out for two weeks, kept between sessions as the unit's carry-out cue. Grade 2 gave a reason; grade 3 backs it with evidence.

Unit 6, Goals that stretch me. Groups rotate four named roles (leader, recorder, checker, timekeeper) on a stretch challenge (a paper tower that holds a book), use the talk turn card, and the student solves one team problem and says what the group did well. Grade 2 had roles; grade 3 rotates four.

Unit 1, Team rules we make. On a team case where a teammate wants to hide a mistake from the teacher, the student uses stop-think-choose to pick the honest action, says how the teammate sees it, and finds a way to be honest that respects them. Grade 4 adds the teammate's view of the honest choice. Checked on the invented case only, never on a student's own conduct.

cross_subject: ela:e4-discussion (the same class talk norms and words)
notes: Unit 1, Team rules we make. Before the class agrees a team norm, the student uses the talk turn card to say back a partner's view and then their own, and checks that the partner feels heard. This year the listener reports the other person's view, not only their words.

Unit 1, Team rules we make. The student reads what a team situation asks of each member (a group presentation, a substitute teacher day) and compares what it asks of them with what it asks of a teammate in another role. New in grade 4: the same moment read for a second person in another role.

Unit 1, Team rules we make. Teams review invented club rules from two sides, a newcomer's and a longtime member's, with the three fairness questions, and agree a version both could accept. Grade 4 adds the second view. Teacher note: invented class, club or game rules only; unfair rules of the past wait for grade 5; no current dispute.

cross_subject: physical-education:g4-team-roles (team roles in games)
notes: Unit 1, Team rules we make. Teams write their own working agreement (how we decide, how we share jobs) and use it on a group build; the student names how a teammate saw a problem differently and how the team used both ideas. The grade 4 turn: a teammate's angle shapes the plan.

Unit 2, Plans and steps. The student reviews a team plan with stop-think-choose, asks a teammate where careful thinking caught a mistake, and writes one place outside school where it would help. Grade 4 adds a partner who points out what the thinking caught.

Unit 2, Plans and steps. For two invented characters with the same hard goal, the student plans two different paths on the goal steps card, each with a helper, and says why one path fits each character better. This year two characters, two paths: what fits one person may not fit another. The course never records a student's own answer.

Unit 2, Plans and steps. Across a two-week team project the student uses the focus plan and its try-again step (try another way, then ask) and checks in with a partner who uses theirs; they compare what pulls each of them off task or stalls them on a hard step, and swap one tip. Grade 4 adds the partner: two plans compared and a tip traded.

cross_subject: health:g4-phw-goal-plan (health plans steps toward a health goal)
notes: Unit 2, Plans and steps. With a partner the student sets a shared goal on the goal steps card, each with their own steps, and changes a step after hearing what blocks the partner. A second person's block now shapes the plan.

words: timeline; deadline; who does what; materials
notes: Unit 2, Plans and steps. The team splits a project into a timeline with deadlines and who does what; the student keeps their own materials list, and at review compares how a teammate planned the same job. Grade 4 adds the team: the plan holds other people's parts and deadlines.

Unit 2, Plans and steps. The student proposes a first step for a team project, asks a teammate's view before starting, and starts it, saying how the other view changed the start. New in grade 4: a teammate's view shapes the first step.

Unit 3, Many ways to be. The student compares two invented characters' identity webs, finds what they share and what differs, and may add to their own private web. Grade 4 sets one web beside another. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

words: strength; language; culture; seen by others
notes: Unit 3, Many ways to be. The student finds a strength a story character brings from their culture or language, and a strength a teammate saw in them, and compares the two views of a strength. Grade 4 adds how another person sees a strength. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 3, Many ways to be. The student gives specific feedback that names a strength the classmate may not see in themselves, and asks how they see it. The grade 4 turn: the classmate's own view of the strength is asked for.

words: point of view; misunderstand; both; shoes switch
cross_subject: ela:e4-narration-pov (first and third person narration compared)
notes: Unit 3, Many ways to be. The student retells a school scene from two characters' points of view with the shoes switch, and writes what each misunderstood about the other. The two sides now meet in one write-up.

Unit 3, Many ways to be. The student checks snap judgments in a case where two characters judge a third differently, finds what each assumed, and uses stop-think-choose to decide what to find out. Grade 4 adds a second judge: two characters, two guesses. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss4-regional-cultures (regions with different ways of life)
notes: Unit 3, Many ways to be. In a project with a story partner whose customs differ, the student plans how to blend two ways of doing a task and asks how the partner sees the blend. This year the partner's view of the blend counts. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

Unit 4, Feelings at work. The student names and rates feelings for two characters in one team scene on the feelings faces scale and explains how the same event made them feel differently. Grade 4 adds a second character: one event, two feelings. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

cross_subject: health:g4-meh-same-thing-different-people (health shows one thing affects people differently)
notes: Unit 4, Feelings at work. The student fills two think-feel-do chains for two characters after the same event (a team loses) with what each character values, and shows how different values and thoughts led to different feelings and actions. Grade 4 runs the chain for two people at once. Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

Unit 4, Feelings at work. In a team scene where two characters' strong feelings collide, the student uses the calm-down steps and says how their response lands on the teammate. New in grade 4: the response is judged by how it lands on someone else.

words: calm-down plan; coach; cue word; cope
cross_subject: health:g4-meh-calm-stress (health applies calming to stress)
notes: Unit 4, Feelings at work. The student builds a calm-down plan for a team moment (a project falling behind) and coaches a partner through theirs with the cue word, noticing which tool works for whom. Grade 4 adds a partner: the student coaches someone else's plan. Teacher note: breathing, stretching and pausing as plain body skills, with no spiritual framing; mental health topics are health's. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 4, Feelings at work. The student uses the care steps for a struggling teammate and adapts when the teammate wants something different from what the student would want. Grade 4 adds the other person's wish, which may differ from the student's own. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 4, Feelings at work. The student reads the clues of two people in a scene on the feelings faces chart and checks in with one in a way that fits that person (quietly, later, with a question). Grade 4 adds the fit: the check-in suits the other person, not the student.

Unit 4, Feelings at work. The team writes thanks to a person who helped the project, from that person's side: what helping cost them and what it made possible. New this year: thanks written from the helper's side.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-levels-of-government (what local and state governments do)
notes: Unit 4, Feelings at work. The student traces how one school or town system (recess rules, a bike lane) shapes what two different people do, such as a student and a crossing guard, and why each might see it differently. Grade 4 adds a second person: one system seen from two places in it.

Unit 5, Leading and following. In a team case where two friends land in different groups, the student repairs the hurt with own it, sorry and a plan, and hears the friend's side first. The student rehearses the repair talk aloud with the I-statement frame while the teacher or a scene card supplies the friend's words and a partner coaches with the step card. Grade 4 adds the friend's side: it is heard before the sorry. Teacher note: no real friends are named.

words: both reasons; compromise; fair; I feel
notes: Unit 5, Leading and following. With a partner, the student works a team disagreement where both sides have good reasons: each says the other's view first, then they use the I-statement frame and find a solution that meets both. Grade 4 adds the other side's view, said before one's own. The teacher plays any upset part.

words: offer; take over; trusted adult; size
cross_subject: health:g4-meh-help-with-feelings (health on getting help with feelings)
notes: Unit 5, Leading and following. The student notices when an invented teammate needs help and offers it without taking over, and sizes a team problem on the problem size meter to know when to bring in a trusted adult. The student rehearses the offer aloud with a partner playing the teammate, then the ask with the partner playing the adult. Grade 4 adds the teammate: help offered so the other person keeps the job. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 5, Leading and following. The student leads a team task with the three leading steps, then follows, and reflects on how leader and follower saw the same decision. This year the leader's and the follower's views of one decision are compared.

cross_subject: health:g4-t-saying-no (health applies refusal to tobacco)
notes: Unit 5, Leading and following. The student rehearses the refusal steps when a card character urges the whole group to break a rule (skip the hard part, blame another team), and holds the no while keeping the friendship. Grade 4 adds the group: the no is held while the friendship is kept. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; no student plays the one who pushes; substance and body-safety topics are health's.

cross_subject: health:g4-v-speak-up-notice (health on noticing and speaking up)
notes: Unit 5, Leading and following. The student plans how a leader and how a follower could each speak up when a teammate is left out, choosing from the upstander options for each role. cross_subject: health:g4-s-decide-with-help (health on deciding with help)

cross_subject: health:g4-fn-food-claims-source-check (health checks a claim against its source)
notes: Unit 6, Thinking it through. The student checks a claim a classmate makes (this snack gives you energy) against facts from a second source, and chooses on what the facts show. This year a second source is checked against a classmate's claim.

Unit 6, Thinking it through. The team solves a school problem by gathering two groups' views (younger students, lunch staff) before choosing and testing a solution. Grade 4 adds other groups' views before the choice.

Owner year for 3 to 5: the steps hold when a change adds pressure.

cross_subject: health:g5-meh-mind-habits (health on habits that help the mind)

Owner year for 3 to 5: an interest weighed against what it costs. Teacher note: the log stays with the student; it is checked only that the steps were followed, never for its content.

Unit 2, What drives me. The student plans a stretch goal for a character facing a setback that costs something (a free afternoon), with two steps, a helper and a backup plan on the goal steps card. Unit 2, What drives me. cross_subject: health:g5-phw-goal-track (health tracks progress toward a goal)
notes: Unit 2, What drives me. The student sets a four-week goal on the goal steps card (it runs inside the unit and is judged at its end), tracks it weekly, and decides what to drop when two goals compete for time. Owner year for 3 to 5: a goal adjusted when two goals compete.

Unit 2, What drives me. The student plans a multi-week project backward from a deadline and recovers when a step slips, saying what the slip cost. Owner year for 3 to 5: a plan built backward that survives a slip.

Unit 3, Who shapes what we do. The student shows on an invented case how careful thinking held up when a group pushed for a fast choice, and what hurrying would have cost. Owner year for 3 to 5: careful thinking held against a group's hurry.

Owner year for 3 to 5: the check held when friends share the guess. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss5-constitution (how a government's rules and rights work)

cross_subject: ela:e5-reasons-to-points (reasons and evidence behind a point)
notes: Unit 3, Who shapes what we do. The student checks a claim like "everyone is doing it" against facts and numbers and chooses on the evidence even when friends lean the other way. Owner year for 3 to 5: the facts chosen over the crowd.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss5-civil-rights-movements (the history of Brown v. Board of Education and the movement)

Teacher note: settled facts the courts have ruled on, taught with dignity; the history is social studies' unit; current political disputes are not SEL content.

cross_subject: health:g5-meh-care-and-kindness (health on care and kindness)

cross_subject: health:g5-v-conflict-steps (health applies conflict steps to health topics)

Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

cross_subject: health:g5-s-speak-up-for-safety (health on speaking up for safety)

Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, and no cause is chosen by the course.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss5-informed-action (social studies on choosing and carrying out an informed action)
notes: Unit 5, My voice, our group. The class proposes a school improvement to the principal or student council with reasons and evidence; the student weighs its time cost and carries out a part. Owner year for 3 to 5: student voice in school life.

cross_subject: computer-science:g5-team-project (team project roles)
notes: Unit 5, My voice, our group. The team works on the school improvement under a deadline and solves a team problem when one member falls behind, without blame. Unit 6, Choices with reach. On an invented case (a friend asks the student to skip the class job to play), the student weighs both people's well-being with stop-think-choose and picks with a reason. Owner year for 3 to 5: the choice holds when friends push the other way.

Unit 6, Choices with reach. The student shows how an invented character's identity stays and changes across a move to a new school. Owner year for 3 to 5: identity followed through a change of school. The student plans how to use their strengths in a new setting (middle school, a new team), identifies an invented character's cultural or linguistic strength and explains how it helps with a new-school task, and adds a strength of their own from a language or culture only if they choose. Owner year for 3 to 5: strengths planned for a setting not yet met. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 6, Choices with reach. Before a big choice in an invented case (where a class trip should go, with the character's friends all set on one place), the student uses the three kinds of question to seek out a view different from the friends' and keeps an open mind when it is unpopular. Owner year for 3 to 5: questions asked when the answer may be unpopular.
Unit 6, Choices with reach. The student solves a community problem the class can act on (litter at the park), weighing what each solution costs. Owner year for 3 to 5: problems beyond the school.

words: short term; long term; many people; judge
cross_subject: health:g5-meh-decision-look-back (health on looking back at a decision)
notes: Unit 6, Choices with reach. Owner year for 3 to 5: results traced for many people and over time.

Unit 1, Finding my way. Unit 1, Finding my way. In a homework scene where a phone keeps buzzing with an invented group chat, the student lists three ways to stay on task (phone in another room, a timer, a study partner), weighs each against what friends expect, picks one and writes the reason, then picks a try-again option for a homework problem that will not come out (reread the worked example, try another way, ask the teacher next day). Step up from grade 5: the focus plan becomes a choice among options against an online pull.

Unit 1, Finding my way. Step up from grade 5: from naming what one new place will ask to choosing an action in places that ask different things.

cross_subject: health:g6-s-reach-reliable-help (health on reaching reliable help and what gets in the way)
notes: Unit 1, Finding my way. Step up from grade 5: from the helper that fits a size to the helper that fits a place and a channel in a school of many adults. Unit 1, Finding my way. The student plans how a character new to middle school could take on a hard first task (a band tryout, a first lab report), chooses between two first steps on the goal steps card, names one place to ask for help and writes why that step comes first. Step up from grade 5: a backup plan becomes a choice between first steps with a reason. Teacher note: the course never records a student's own answer; checks use the character's plan.

Unit 2, Who am I now?. The student maps the roles and groups of an invented sixth grader (a team, family chores, an online game club, a language spoken at home), chooses which parts the character shows in two settings and writes why. Step up from grade 5: from how identity stays and changes across a move to choosing what to show in different groups. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 2, Who am I now?. The student matches an invented character's strengths, one of them from a home language, to three new-school tasks, picks where each helps most and writes the reason. Unit 2, Who am I now?. In a case where a character forgot a group task and friends offer an easy excuse, the student lays out the options on stop-think-choose, picks the honest one, names the value behind it and writes what it may cost with friends. Unit 2, Who am I now?. The student lists new interests a middle school offers (clubs, electives, a sport), weighs two against time and what friends pick, and privately chooses one to try with a written reason. Step up from grade 5: from naming mixed feelings to choosing the exact word and its strength. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

Unit 2, Who am I now?. The student fills the think-feel-do chain for a character who reads a friend's short reply in an invented chat as anger, names what the character values (being included) and how it shapes that reading, writes two other possible thoughts, picks the one the facts best support and writes why. Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

Step up from grade 5: the steps used to choose among responses, with onlookers as the pressure.

cross_subject: health:g6-meh-stress-coping (health teaches stress and coping as a health topic)
notes: Unit 3, Stress and strong feelings. The grades 3 to 5 calm-down steps gain a fifth step, go on: stop, breathe, name it, choose, go on (choose is choosing a tool). Unit 3, Stress and strong feelings. The student reads an invented practice log of a character stuck on a skill (free throws, a hard piece of music), lists three changes (a new strategy, feedback from a coach, spaced practice), picks one and writes why the log points to it. Never belief alone. Step up from grade 5: from explaining a setback to choosing the fix among options.

Unit 3, Stress and strong feelings. The stop-think-choose card grows to five steps for 6 to 8: stop, list options, weigh each, choose, write the reason. The student uses it on a crowded night in a story (three assignments due, a friend asking for help the same evening) and shows in writing where careful thinking changed the choice. Step up from grade 5: careful thinking done on options laid side by side.

Unit 3, Stress and strong feelings. The student weighs an invented character's choice between a late online game with friends and sleep before a test, for the character's own well-being and for teammates counting on them, and writes the reason for the pick. Step up from grade 5: well-being weighed across several options, with online time as the pull.

cross_subject: health:g6-t-when-careful-decision (health applies careful choosing to nicotine pressure)

cross_subject: math:m6-summarize-data (summarizing a data set before drawing a conclusion)
