Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

Unit 5, Online and offline norms. The student writes specific credit for a classmate's work on an invented class project page and chooses between public and private praise, with a reason. Step up from grade 5: credit given in a chosen setting, online included.

Unit 5, Online and offline norms. The student maps who an invented post could reach (friends, strangers, the person in it, the school) and which school rules it touches, then picks among options with the reason. Step up from grade 5: the map of who is affected reaches an online audience.

cross_subject: health:g6-phw-goal-alone-or-with (health on goals pursued alone or with support)
notes: Unit 6, Goals and our team. The student sets a goal for the term on the goal steps card, chooses between working at it alone or with a partner, weighs it against time for clubs and friends, and writes the reason. Step up from grade 5: choosing how to pursue a goal, not only tracking it.

Unit 6, Goals and our team. The student chooses among three ways an invented sixth grader could step forward in a team project (offer a plan, take a role nobody wants, draw in a quiet member) and writes why, then plans the first step on the goal steps card. Step up from grade 5: starting by choosing among roles.

Unit 6, Goals and our team. The class drafts a proposal to improve a sixth-grade routine (the lunch line, locker time); the student weighs two ways to present it (a letter, a short talk to the student council) and carries out a part. Step up from grade 5: student voice in school life with a chosen route.

cross_subject: physical-education:g6-welcome-differences (respecting differences among teammates)
notes: Unit 6, Goals and our team. In an invented mixed team from different elementary schools and backgrounds, the student chooses among ways to settle a clash of ways of working (how to split work, when to talk), one teammate's way drawn from a cited cultural or education source and shown as that one student's way, and writes the reason. Step up from grade 5: respect shown by choosing how to adjust. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

cross_subject: computer-science:g6-inclusive-collab (pair roles and giving credit in a team)
notes: Unit 6, Goals and our team. The team chooses how to divide a project among options (by strength, by rotation, by choice) and solves a time problem when a member has a game the night before the deadline, writing why the split was fair. Step up from grade 5: the split itself chosen and defended.

Unit 6, Goals and our team. The student leads a team choice by picking a way to decide (a vote, consensus, the leader decides) that fits the decision, writes why, then follows a decision they argued against. Step up from grade 5: leading by choosing how the group decides.

cross_subject: health:g6-v-bullying-harassment-help (health on bullying, cyberbullying and getting help)
notes: Unit 6, Goals and our team. The grades 3 to 5 upstander plan gains "report online", for four options (speak up, support the person afterward, get an adult, report online). The student chooses the safest for an invented case of a student mocked in a team chat, rehearses the chosen words with a partner while the teacher or a card plays the one posting the mockery (the I-statement frame for a speak-up, the plain facts for a report), and writes why. Step up from grade 5: from the four-option plan offline to the same plan with a report online and the safest option chosen for a team chat. Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, and no cause is chosen by the course.

Unit 6, Goals and our team. The class picks a school problem (a crowded hallway between classes); the student lists solutions on stop-think-choose, sizes the problem on the meter, weighs solutions against criteria (cost, time, who it helps) and writes the pick and reason. Step up from grade 5: solutions weighed against stated criteria.

Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. The student compares how two invented seventh graders see the same group (one belongs to the team, one is new to it), and chooses how each could show who they are there, with the reason. Grade 7 adds the other person's view of belonging. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. The student sets a partner's list of an invented teammate's strengths beside the teammate's own list, and chooses which strength the group should lean on, writing why. New this year: how others see a strength. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

words: shared interest; pull; own choice; purpose
notes: Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. Privately the student weighs an interest a friend group shares against one only they care about, and writes which to give time to and why. What grade 7 adds: another person's pull on the choice. Teacher note: the list stays with the student; it is checked only that the steps were followed, never for its content.

words: trust; balance; new group; both sides
notes: Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. When one invented friend joins a new group, the student writes how the friendship looks from each friend's side, chooses what to say with the I-statement frame, rehearses it with a partner playing the friend who joined the new group, and writes why. This year the friend's side is weighed with one's own. Teacher note: no real friends are named; dating and relationship health topics are health's.

Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. In an invented mixed team, the student takes the other partner's view of a clash over how blunt feedback should be (one partner's way from a cited source on feedback customs, shown as that student's own), chooses how both could adapt, and writes the reason. Grade 7 asks students to see their own habits as a partner might. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. The student notices strengths in an invented group member others overlook, imagines how that member would hear praise, and chooses words that will land. The other person's view now shapes the credit.

cross_subject: physical-education:g7-game-plans-feedback (specific feedback on a team plan)
notes: Unit 1, Belonging and our groups. The team gives and takes feedback on a shared plan; the student hears a teammate's view of how the work was split, changes one role and writes why. New in grade 7: a teammate's sense of fairness reshapes the plan.

words: pressure; peer; alternative; keep the friend
cross_subject: health:g7-aod-turn-down-requests (health applies refusal to alcohol and drug requests)
notes: Unit 2, Under pressure. The student rehearses the refusal options against a card character in an invented group chat who presses them to forward a mean meme that mocks a student's drawing, then thinks through how the pushing friend sees it and offers an alternative that keeps the friendship. What changes: the other side's view helps pick the refusal. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; no student plays the one who pushes and no real classmate is named; substance, body-safety and dating topics are health's (health row g7-aod-turn-down-requests takes the substance cases).

Unit 2, Under pressure. The student reads an invented situation (an invitation from older students to sit with them at a game, a group dare at the park) from their own side and from a parent's or friend's side, chooses how to act on stop-think-choose, and writes what each side would want. Grade 7 reads the moment through someone else's eyes.

Unit 2, Under pressure. The student traces how an invented trend spreads on a video app and how it looks to the person the trend makes fun of, then writes which app rule would change what people do. This year adds the view of the person a norm hurts. Teacher note: invented apps, accounts and posts only, never the student's own; no product names.

Unit 2, Under pressure. The student predicts how a choice under pressure (joining an invented prank on a substitute teacher) plays out for themselves and for the person on the other end, and chooses with the reason written. Grade 7 puts the other person's results into the weighing.

Unit 2, Under pressure. During an invented study session with a friend who wants to chat, the student chooses a focus option that also respects the friend (a set break, a shared timer) and a try-again option for the hardest part of the study task (try another way, explain it to the friend), and writes why on the goal steps card. The pull is now a person whose view counts.

Unit 3, Snap judgments. Main year for snap judgments in 6 to 8 (STANDARD section 3). The student notices a snap judgment in an invented case (a character decides a new student will not fit the team because of how they dress), writes how the judged student would experience the guess, and checks it against evidence before choosing what to do. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

cross_subject: ela:e7-contrast-pov (contrasting the points of view of characters)
notes: Unit 3, Snap judgments. The student retells an invented clash from the view of each person in it, names the motive each might have, and chooses what to ask before judging. Grade 7 holds two full points of view at once, where grade 6 held one.

Unit 3, Snap judgments. Main year for unfair norms in 6 to 8. The student uses the three fairness questions on an invented club rule and on a settled change to a national norm (the Nineteenth Amendment, 1920, after which the vote could no longer be denied on account of sex), takes the view of the people each norm left out, and chooses a fair change with the reason. Here the second person is the one the norm left out. Teacher note: settled history, taught with dignity from a federal archive page and the community's own account; current political disputes are not SEL content.

words: open mind; other side; best case; curious
notes: Unit 3, Snap judgments. Before a class vote the student talks with a partner who holds the other view, writes the best version of that view, and decides whether it changes their own, with the reason. New this year: the other side's case written out in full.

cross_subject: math:m7-random-samples (a random sample standing for a population)
notes: Unit 3, Snap judgments. The student checks two invented claims about what most seventh graders think against a small random sample, decides which claim the data back, and writes why each person might have believed theirs. Grade 7 adds why the other person believes what they do.

Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. The student names an invented character's inside feeling and the feeling the character shows, as another character would see it, rates both on the scale, and chooses words to ask about the gap. Grade 7 asks what one person's feeling looks like to another. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. The student fills two think-feel-do chains for the same invented moment, one for each person in it, and writes how each person's value (fairness, belonging) and thought changed their feeling and action. This year the chain runs for both people. Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

cross_subject: physical-education:g7-manage-feelings (managing frustration and stress in games)
notes: Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. In an invented scene where a teammate's mistake loses a game, the student uses the calm-down steps, chooses a response, and writes how the teammate would hear each option. What grade 7 adds: how a response lands on the other person.

Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. The student coaches a partner through choosing a tool from the menu for an invented stressful moment, notices the partner may need a different tool than their own, and writes how two friends could agree on a calm signal. New in grade 7: helping another person choose. Teacher note: breathing, stretching and pausing as plain body skills, with no spiritual framing. Stress, sleep and mental health topics are health's (health row g6-meh-stress-coping), named in the teacher notes. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. The student chooses the true action in an invented case where a friend asks them to cover for a broken rule, writes how the friend and the teacher each see it, and names what honesty costs. Grade 7 sets honesty against loyalty to another person. Checked on the invented case only, never on a student's own conduct.

Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. When an invented friend doubts they can pass a hard test, the student names two steps the friend could take and one place to ask for help on the goal steps card, and writes what they would say to encourage. Grade 7 turns the skill outward, to another person's doubt. Teacher note: the course never records a student's own answer; checks use the character's plan.

Unit 4, Big feelings, steady choices. The student reads feedback a coach gave an invented player, takes the coach's view of what to change, and chooses the practice plan with the reason. Never belief alone. This year the fix starts from someone else's feedback.

cross_subject: ela:e7-collab-discussion (acknowledging others' ideas and modifying one's own in discussion)
notes: Unit 5, Repair and conflict. The student listens to a partner's account of an invented misunderstanding and sums it up until the partner agrees, then gives their own side with the talk turn card. Grade 7 makes the other person the judge of whether they were heard.

cross_subject: health:g7-v-conflict-prevent-end (health on preventing and ending conflict)
notes: Unit 5, Repair and conflict. With a partner the student works an invented conflict by naming each side's interests, choosing a repair (an apology, a fix, a new plan), and saying the I-statement. New this year: the other side's interests shape the repair. The teacher plays any upset part.

cross_subject: health:g7-meh-seek-and-give-support (health on seeking and giving support)
notes: Unit 5, Repair and conflict. The student notices an invented friend who is struggling but has not asked, sizes the problem on the meter, chooses how to offer help, rehearses the offer with a partner playing the friend (who first turns it down), knows when to bring in an adult even if the friend says no, and writes why the chosen offer fits. Grade 7 is about offering from the other person's side. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor. Self-harm and crisis topics are health's (health row g7-meh-self-harm-help).

Unit 5, Repair and conflict. Before acting, the student asks what an invented struggling friend wants (company, help, space), and writes how the friend would feel about each kind of care. The friend's own wish now decides the care. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

words: signal; mixed message; both people; respect
notes: Unit 5, Repair and conflict. The student reads the feelings of both people in an invented argument from their clues, checks in with each, and chooses words that respect each side. Grade 7 reads two people at once.

Unit 5, Repair and conflict. After an invented conflict is settled, the student thanks the other person for something they did in the repair, choosing words that person will take as sincere. New in grade 7: thanks as part of repair, aimed at how the other person hears it.

cross_subject: health:g7-s-spot-speak-up (health on spotting chances to speak up)
notes: Unit 5, Repair and conflict. The student plans how to support the person treated unfairly in an invented case, asks what that person wants before acting, and chooses the upstander option they would welcome. The student rehearses the check-in question and the chosen words with the teacher, who plays the person treated unfairly and then the unkind act, while a partner watches for the steps; then the student writes why that option fits. Grade 7 adds the target's own view. Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, and no cause is chosen by the course.

Unit 5, Repair and conflict. The student leads a group through an invented disagreement as a neutral guide with the talk turn card, making sure each side is heard, then follows the group's choice. This year the leader holds everyone's view, not their own.

cross_subject: health:g7-phw-write-goal-link (health writes measurable goals)
notes: Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student sets a shared goal with a partner on the goal steps card, weighs both partners' time against it, and changes the plan after a check-in where the partner's needs differ. Grade 7: a partner's needs reshape the choice.

Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student plans an invented team event timeline where others' tasks depend on theirs, builds in a buffer, and writes how a late teammate changes the plan. What grade 7 adds: depending on other people.

Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student starts a class project and invites a classmate who would not join on their own, writing how the project looks from that classmate's side. New this year: bringing another person in.

Unit 6, Taking the lead. The class drafts a proposal for a school change, and the student asks two groups it affects (younger students, staff) what they think and changes the proposal with the reason. Grade 7: the proposal answers other people's views.

Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student solves a school problem with an invented group that disagrees on its cause, records each person's view of the cause, and chooses a solution to test, writing the reason. Other people's views of the cause enter this year.

Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student runs the five-step stop-think-choose with a partner who prefers a different option, and writes how hearing the partner's reasons changed or held the choice. Careful thinking now takes in another person's reasons.

Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student weighs an invented choice between a weekend team practice and a family chore day, for their own well-being and for the people on each side, writing how each would see it. Grade 7 gives the other people's well-being its own column.

cross_subject: computer-science:g7-impact-history (intended and unintended effects on people)
notes: Unit 6, Taking the lead. The student maps who a class decision affects, then asks a partner playing one affected group for an effect they missed, and chooses with the reason. Grade 7 adds a voice from the affected side.

cross_subject: ela:e8-conflicting-viewpoints (answering conflicting viewpoints)
notes: Unit 1, How I decide. The student questions two invented sources that disagree on a school issue, stays open while friends have already picked a side, and writes a choice and reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: openness kept when it costs standing with friends.

cross_subject: health:g8-phw-handle-false-messages (health on handling false health messages)
notes: Unit 1, How I decide. The student checks a fast-spreading invented rumor against facts and numbers before a deadline to respond, and chooses on the evidence when the popular view leans the other way, writing the reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: evidence weighed under time and social pressure.

cross_subject: health:g8-pa-decision-look-back (health on judging a decision afterward)
notes: Unit 1, How I decide. The student weighs short- and long-term costs of options in an invented case (quitting a team for more free time), chooses, and later judges the choice against how the story turns out. Owner year for 6 to 8: a choice where every option costs something.

Unit 1, How I decide. The student runs stop-think-choose with a two-minute limit on an invented case, then reflects in writing on where the clock bent the thinking and what a longer pause would have changed. Owner year for 6 to 8: careful thinking against a clock.

words: thought trap; pressure; slow down; choose
notes: Unit 1, How I decide. The student fills the think-feel-do chain for a character pushed to decide fast (an invented group chat demanding an answer now), writes a thought that slows the chain, explains how what the character values (keeping a promise, fitting in) pulls the thought each way, and chooses. Owner year for 6 to 8: the chain changed while pressure pushes. Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

Unit 1, How I decide. The student maps who a choice affects near and far when it is popular with friends but costs another group, and writes the pick with the reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: weighing everyone affected when it costs popularity.

Unit 2, Values and integrity. The student chooses the true action in an invented case where honesty costs a team its win (a missed call in its favor), and names the value behind it and the price. Owner year for 6 to 8: honesty with a real loss attached. Checked on the invented case only, never on a student's own conduct.

Unit 2, Values and integrity. The student shows how an invented eighth grader keeps their values across groups that want different things, and chooses what to hold to when one group pushes. Owner year for 6 to 8: identity held under group pressure. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 2, Values and integrity. The student plans how an invented character could use a strength where showing it costs something (being called a try-hard), explains how a second invented character's cultural or linguistic strength helps the team's task despite that cost, and writes the choice and reason; a student's own strength is added only if they choose. Owner year for 6 to 8: a strength used despite a social cost. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 2, Values and integrity. The student checks a snap judgment an invented friend group already shares about a new student, chooses a fair action though disagreeing costs standing, and writes the reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: a fair action chosen against a group's shared guess. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

cross_subject: health:g8-aod-refusal-and-driving (health applies refusal to unsafe rides)
notes: Unit 2, Values and integrity. Owner year for 6 to 8: a no held when it costs. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; no student plays the one who pushes and no real classmate is named; substance, body-safety and dating topics are health's (health row g8-aod-refusal-and-driving takes the unsafe-ride case).

Unit 2, Values and integrity. The student reads an invented situation whose stakes rise (a game at the park turns into a dare), chooses on stop-think-choose whether to stay, change it or leave, and writes what each costs. Owner year for 6 to 8: reading a moment as the pressure climbs.

Unit 2, Values and integrity. Privately the student weighs whether an interest is worth what it takes (dropping another activity, time with friends) and writes a purpose for keeping or dropping it. Owner year for 6 to 8: keep or drop weighed against real costs, in writing. Teacher note: the list stays with the student; it is checked only that the steps were followed, never for its content.

Unit 2, Values and integrity. The student plans how an invented character could take on a challenge where failing would be public (a solo at a concert), with two steps, a helper and what to do if it goes wrong, on the goal steps card. Owner year for 6 to 8: belief acted on when failure has a cost. Teacher note: the course never records a student's own answer; checks use the character's plan.

Unit 3, Stress, focus and rest. The student names and rates the feelings of an invented student through a heavy week (tests, a game, a family event), choosing exact words as the strength rises, and writes the clue for each. Owner year for 6 to 8: feelings named as pressure builds. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

Unit 3, Stress, focus and rest. The student plans practice for an invented skill when time is short, choosing among more practice, better practice and asking for help, and writes why rest belongs in the plan. Never belief alone. Owner year for 6 to 8: growth planned under a time cost. Also carries AASL.V.D.2 (skill grows with practice and help), placed in SEL by library (docs/courses/library/STANDARD.md section 4); it moves into the standard cell once scripts/progression.py accepts AASL ids for SEL.

Unit 3, Stress, focus and rest. In a high-stakes invented scene (a tryout, a public mistake), the student uses the calm-down steps, picks a response from options, rehearses the steps and the response in a short scene, and writes what reacting would cost and how to recover. Owner year for 6 to 8: a response chosen when the stakes are high, with a plan to recover.

words: routine; sleep; screen time; coping plan
notes: Unit 3, Stress, focus and rest. The student builds a weekly coping plan for an invented busy student that weighs sleep, screen time and practice, chooses tools from the menu, and writes what each choice costs. Owner year for 6 to 8: coping chosen when every option takes time. Teacher note: breathing, stretching and pausing as plain body skills, with no spiritual framing. Stress, sleep and mental health topics are health's (health rows g6-meh-stress-coping and g7-phw-sleep-habits-community), named in the teacher notes. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 3, Stress, focus and rest. The student keeps an invented long project on track through a week with a game and a group chat that will not quiet down, chooses what to put off and writes the cost, and makes a try-again plan for the hardest part of the project, chosen from options (try another way, break it smaller, ask for help) with the reason written. Owner year for 6 to 8: focus held against both time and friends, and through the hard part. Also carries AASL.V.D.1 (trying again when a task gets hard), placed in SEL by library (docs/courses/library/STANDARD.md section 4); it moves into the standard cell once scripts/progression.py accepts AASL ids for SEL.

Unit 3, Stress, focus and rest. The student plans an invented week where commitments clash (homework, a team, a family chore), decides what to cut or move, writes the cost of each choice, and keeps the project's papers and materials in a chosen system (a folder by due date, a checklist), with how it supports the revised week. Owner year for 6 to 8: planning when not everything fits.

cross_subject: health:g8-meh-different-views (health on respecting different views)
notes: Unit 4, Understanding others. The student states the view of an invented person whose values differ on a school issue well enough that the person would agree with the summary, even when friends mock that view. Owner year for 6 to 8: taking a view that costs something to take.

cross_subject: health:g8-meh-express-concern (health on expressing concern for a friend)
notes: Unit 4, Understanding others. The student plans care for an invented friend whose hard time goes on, including when caring costs time or the friend's annoyance, and when to bring in an adult. Owner year for 6 to 8: care kept up over time, with the point where an adult comes in. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor. Crisis topics are health's (health row g8-meh-suicide-help).

Unit 4, Understanding others. The student reads feelings in an invented group conversation where cues hide behind jokes and short replies, chooses among responses one that may cost a laugh but respects the person, and writes the reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: cues read under the group's laughter.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-civil-rights-laws (the civil rights laws that changed unfair norms)
notes: Unit 4, Understanding others. The student uses the fairness questions on a settled disability-access change (Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, 1973, or the Americans with Disabilities Act, 1990), names what changing the norm cost the people who pressed for it, and sets beside it an invented school norm that someone would pay a price to change. Owner year for 6 to 8: the price of changing a norm, in settled history and in school. The history itself is social studies' (ss8-civil-rights-laws).

words: difference; common ground; give up; deadline
notes: Unit 4, Understanding others. In an invented team of Deaf and hearing students whose ways of communicating differ (signing through an interpreter, written chat, faces visible when talking) with a deadline close, the student asks for and respects each preference, chooses how to find common ground and writes what each side gives up; case cards only, no simulation of hearing loss (source: the Deaf-Hearing Communication Centre's communication tips). Owner year for 6 to 8: respect kept when time is short. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

Unit 4, Understanding others. The student gives specific credit to an invented rival team or classmate even when it costs a little pride, and writes why it matters. Owner year for 6 to 8: credit given to a rival, at a cost to pride.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-news-literacy (how news media shape what people know)
notes: Unit 4, Understanding others. The student traces how an invented school system and an invented app each reward some behavior, names the pressure each puts on students, and writes one change and what it would cost. Owner year for 6 to 8: a school system and an online one weighed side by side, with the cost of a change. Teacher note: invented apps, accounts and posts only, never the student's own; no product names.

cross_subject: ela:e8-collab-discussion (qualifying and justifying views in discussion)
notes: Unit 5, Communication and conflict. The student uses the talk turn card in an invented hard talk where speaking plainly may cost a friendship, choosing the channel and the words, and writes the reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: the channel and the words chosen when plain talk may cost a friendship.

Unit 5, Communication and conflict. The student weighs an invented friendship where staying close costs other friends or values, chooses whether to set a limit or step back, rehearses the I-statement with a partner playing the friend, and writes the choice and its reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: a friendship choice with a price on each side. Teacher note: no real friends are named; dating and relationship health topics are health's.

cross_subject: health:g8-v-negotiate-compromise (health on negotiating a compromise)
notes: Unit 5, Communication and conflict. With a partner the student negotiates an invented disagreement where any deal costs both sides, chooses a compromise and writes why it is fair. Owner year for 6 to 8: a negotiated deal where both sides pay. The teacher plays any upset part.

words: reluctant; trusted adult; worry; follow through
notes: Unit 5, Communication and conflict. The student plans asking for help when it costs (admitting a mistake, a friend's secret that worries them) and offering help that takes real time, sizing each on the meter and choosing whom to go to from options, rehearses each ask aloud with a partner playing the adult or the friend, and writes the reason for the choice. Owner year for 6 to 8: help sought and given when it has a price. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor. Unit 5, Communication and conflict. The student thanks someone in an invented case whose help cost them (a teammate who gave up a spot), choosing words and timing. Owner year for 6 to 8: thanks for help that had a price.

words: long-term goal; monitor; setback; give up
cross_subject: health:g8-phw-goal-monitor (health on monitoring and adjusting a goal)
notes: Unit 6, Making a difference. The student sets a term goal, monitors it on the goal steps card, and adjusts when it competes with friends and time, writing what was given up; the goal is checked at the unit's end and carried on as the unit's carry-out cue. Owner year for 6 to 8: a goal kept against friends and time, with the trade written down.

Unit 6, Making a difference. For a school improvement that may cost time and draw teasing, the student chooses between two first steps (ask the student council, or start a sign-up sheet), writes why the chosen one fits the cost, starts it on the goal steps card and recruits others. Owner year for 6 to 8: starting when starting is costly.

cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-civic-action (deliberating and carrying out an informed action)
notes: Unit 6, Making a difference. The class proposes and carries out a school improvement; the student weighs its costs for different groups, answers objections and does a part. Owner year for 6 to 8: student voice in school life, with no cause picked by the course.

cross_subject: health:g8-meh-teamwork (health on team roles and cooperation)
notes: Unit 6, Making a difference. The team carries the project under a real deadline; when a member's absence costs everyone, the student chooses among three ways to cover the absent member's part (share it out, cut its scope, ask for more time) and writes the reason, without blame. Owner year for 6 to 8: a gap in the team covered by a weighed choice. Also carries AASL.III.D.2 (the group's learning as one's own job), placed in SEL by library (docs/courses/library/STANDARD.md section 4); it moves into the standard cell once scripts/progression.py accepts AASL ids for SEL.

cross_subject: physical-education:g8-leading (leading a group in activity)
notes: Unit 6, Making a difference. The student leads a decision that will be unpopular with part of the team and follows a leader they disagree with, writing what each cost. Owner year for 6 to 8: leading and following at a cost to the team's goodwill.

Unit 6, Making a difference. On an invented case where speaking up costs standing with friends (the group keeps replaying a classmate's stumble from a school video), the student chooses the safest of the upstander options, rehearses the words with a partner, using the I-statement frame, while the teacher or a card plays the unkind act, and writes why that option fits the cost. Owner year for 6 to 8: speaking up chosen and weighed when it costs standing with friends. Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, and no cause is chosen by the course.

Unit 6, Making a difference. The class solves a community problem it can act on, weighs solutions against cost and time on stop-think-choose, chooses one and judges it afterward. Owner year for 6 to 8: problems where the fix has a cost.

Unit 6, Making a difference. The student weighs a choice for their own and others' well-being when it costs something they want (a trip with friends against a promise to help a neighbor), and writes the reason. Owner year for 6 to 8: well-being weighed when it costs something wanted.

Unit 1, A new start. The goal steps card grows for 9 to 12 into a plan the student designs: the goal, dated steps, the trade-off accepted, a check date and a verdict on how well it worked. The student designs a planning system for an invented first month of high school (seven classes, a team, a long-term project), names what the system gives up (a paper planner is slower, a phone calendar distracts), follows it through a two-week case calendar and judges what held and what to change. Step up from grade 8: from cutting and moving clashing commitments to building and testing a whole system.

Unit 1, A new start. The student designs a focus plan for an invented ninth grader with a project due in three weeks and no one checking daily: chosen work blocks, what to do about the phone, a self check-in each Friday. The student writes the trade-off of the plan and, after reading how the character's first week went, judges which part worked and rewrites one. Step up from grade 8: the student builds the focus plan rather than choosing what to put off in one week.

Unit 1, A new start. The stop-think-choose card gains a sixth step for 9 to 12: look back, judge how the choice worked and what to change. The student reads three invented high-school settings (a first lab with a new partner, a club fair, a hallway where older students gather), plans how to act in each with what each choice opens and closes, then judges the plan against how the case turned out. Step up from grade 8: from reading rising stakes in one moment to planning across settings and judging the plan.

words: support map; resource; counselor; follow up
cross_subject: health:g9-meh-help-and-concern (health applies asking for and giving help to health concerns)
notes: Unit 1, A new start. The problem size meter grows into a support map for 9 to 12: each size of problem beside the people and offices that fit it, in school and out. The student builds a support map for an invented new high-school student (a missed assignment, a schedule error, a worry that keeps coming back), plans how to ask in each case and what to do if the first helper cannot help, rehearses one ask aloud with a partner playing the adult or office, then judges whether the map covers the cases. Step up from grade 8: from planning one costly ask to designing a map of where help is. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor. Crisis topics are health's (health row g9-meh-suicide-and-self-harm-help).

Unit 1, A new start. The student designs a plan for an invented ninth grader taking on a course that feels too hard: two first steps, a place to ask for help, what the character will count as progress, and the trade-off (less free time). After reading the character's first test result, the student judges the plan and names one change. Step up from grade 8: belief turned into a designed plan with its own test. Teacher note: the course never records a student's own answer; checks use the character's plan.

cross_subject: computer-science:g9-career-interests (listing a goal and the skills it needs)
notes: Unit 1, A new start. Privately the student plans how to explore two interests a high school offers (a course, a club, a job shadow day), with what each costs in time and what it might give, then after a set date judges whether the plan helped them find a purpose. Step up from grade 8: from weighing one interest's worth to designing a small test of interests. Teacher note: the list stays with the student; it is checked only that the steps were followed, never for its content.

Unit 2, Stress and coping. The feelings scale adds two parts for 9 to 12: what set the feeling off and what it pushes toward, so a plan can meet it early. The student charts an invented student's feelings across a school week (a test, a missed bus, good news), finds a pattern and plans where an early sign could be caught, then judges whether the chart showed enough to plan from. Step up from grade 8: from naming feelings as pressure builds to reading a pattern and planning for it. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

Unit 2, Stress and coping. The student designs a response plan for an invented student who snaps at people after hard practices: the trigger, the early sign on the feelings scale, a calm-down step, a planned response and a repair if it goes wrong. The student names what the plan costs (leaving a moment early) and judges it against a second scene. Step up from grade 8: from choosing one response in a high-stakes moment to a plan made ahead.

cross_subject: health:g9-meh-influences-judge-plan (health designs a plan for the influences on health)
notes: Unit 2, Stress and coping. The calm-down steps become a coping plan the student designs for 9 to 12: the five steps, a tool for each of three settings, a back-up tool and a review date. The student builds the plan for an invented student's heavy week (tests, a game, extra family chores), rehearses two tools with a partner, names what each costs and judges after the case week which tool fit. Step up from grade 8: from a weekly plan chosen from the menu to a plan built and judged. Teacher note: breathing, stretching and pausing as plain body skills, with no spiritual framing. Stress and mental health topics are health's (health rows g9-meh-influences-judge-plan and g9-meh-suicide-and-self-harm-help), named in the teacher notes. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

Unit 2, Stress and coping. The student maps the think-feel-do loop of an invented student who reads a low quiz grade as "I am bad at this", with what the student cares about (doing well for a coach, being seen as capable) shown as part of the loop, plans where to break the loop (a checked thought, a talk with the teacher), and judges the plan by how the next scene goes. Step up from grade 8: from slowing one chain under pressure to planning where to break a loop that repeats. Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

cross_subject: physical-education:g9-skill-practice-plan (setting a skill goal and planning practice)
notes: Unit 2, Stress and coping. The student designs a practice plan on the goal steps card for a skill an invented student finds hard (a language's verb forms, a drum pattern): what to practice, how often, who gives feedback, when to rest and how to measure progress, then judges the plan from a made-up log of three weeks. Never belief alone. Step up from grade 8: from choosing among ways to practice to designing and testing the whole plan.

Unit 2, Stress and coping. The class picks a school-day stressor it can act on (a crowded test week, a noisy study hall); the student writes the problem plainly, sizes it on the meter, designs a fix with its trade-offs, runs a small pilot where the school allows, and judges with the look-back step whether it helped. Step up from grade 8: from weighing solutions to a community problem to piloting a designed one and judging it.

words: identity; role; steady; change over time
notes: Unit 3, Identity and assets. The student writes a short identity sketch for an invented ninth grader (or one they make up): the roles and groups that make up the person, which parts the character plans to keep steady in high school and which to try changing, with the trade-off of each, then judges the sketch after a scene where two groups pull different ways. Step up from grade 8: from holding values under group push to planning how identity grows. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 3, Identity and assets. The student lists an invented character's assets (a skill, a habit, a language spoken at home, a talent from a hobby), plans where each could help in a new school year, names a strength that may be undervalued there, and judges which match was strongest. Step up from grade 8: from using one strength at a cost to an asset plan across settings. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 3, Identity and assets. The student designs how an invented student could act on a value where honesty is awkward (a group project where one member copied work): what to say and to whom, what the honest path costs, and a judgment of the plan with the look-back step. Step up from grade 8: from choosing the true action at a price to planning how to carry it out. Checked on the invented case only, never on a student's own conduct.

Unit 3, Identity and assets. The student plans how an invented ninth grader could test a snap judgment about a new lab partner (what to ask, what evidence would change it), runs the case and judges whether the plan caught the error. Step up from grade 8: from checking a judgment a group shares to a plan for testing one's own. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

Unit 3, Identity and assets. For an invented project team from different backgrounds and schools, the student designs working rules that respect each member's habits (how to disagree, how fast to reply), names what each member adapts, and judges the rules after a scene where they are tested. Step up from grade 8: from finding common ground on a deadline to designing team rules ahead. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

words: check back; main point; tone; channel
cross_subject: ela:e9-sl-discussion (the same discussion norms and evidence moves)
notes: Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. The talk turn card adds a last step for 9 to 12: check what landed (the listener says back the main point) and plan the next talk. The student plans a hard school-day talk on an invented case (telling a lab partner the work split is unfair), rehearses it with a partner, and judges from the check-back whether the meaning got across. Step up from grade 8: from choosing channel and words to planning and checking the whole talk.

words: healthy; give and take; limit; check-in
notes: Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. The I-statement frame keeps the 6 to 8 words and adds a check-back as a fifth part for 9 to 12: I feel ___ when ___ because ___. I need ___. Does that work for you? The student sorts signs of healthy and unhealthy friendship in an invented case (a friend who copies homework and gets angry when asked to stop), plans a talk with the frame and a limit, rehearses the talk while the teacher or a scene card supplies the angry friend's words and a partner coaches with the card, and judges the plan by the scene's end. Step up from grade 8: from choosing to step back to designing what to say and what limit to hold. Teacher note: no real friends are named; dating and relationship health topics are health's (health rows g9-v-abuse-and-dating-violence and g9-sh-health-and-consent).

cross_subject: health:g9-v-conflict-manage (health applies calm, listen and negotiate steps to preventing violence)
notes: Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. With a partner the student works an invented disagreement over a shared school task: plans the talk, names each side's interests, offers two options, agrees one with the I-statement frame and sets a follow-up check, then judges the agreement after the case's next week. Step up from grade 8: from negotiating one compromise to planning a fix and checking it held. The teacher plays any upset part.

cross_subject: health:g9-aod-say-no-across (health applies refusal to parties, rides and jobs)
notes: Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. The student designs a refusal plan for an invented school-day pressure (a friend pushing to share test answers in a group chat): the refusal options, an exit, an ally to bring in and the value it rests on, then rehearses it against a card character and judges which part held. Step up from grade 8: from holding one costly no to a plan made before the pressure arrives. Teacher note: the teacher or a card plays the pressure; no student plays the one who pushes and no real classmate is named; substance, sexual health and dating topics are health's (health rows g9-aod-say-no-across, g9-sh-health-and-consent and g9-v-abuse-and-dating-violence).

words: support plan; ask first; space; adult
notes: Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. The student plans support for an invented classmate going through a hard few weeks at school (a lost spot on the team): what to ask first, what kinds of care to offer, when to step back and when to bring in an adult, then judges the plan against how the friend responds. Step up from grade 8: from planning care that costs to a support plan with checkpoints. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor. Crisis topics are health's (health row g9-meh-suicide-and-self-harm-help).

cross_subject: physical-education:g9-courtesy-aware (being aware of how others feel during activity)
notes: Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. The student reads cues in an invented school-day scene (a friend quiet at lunch, short replies after class), plans a check-in with two possible openings, and judges which reading was right once the case reveals more. Step up from grade 8: from reading hidden cues in a group to planning a check-in and testing the reading.

Unit 4, Relationships that are good for me. The student designs a small gratitude habit for an invented student's school week (who to thank, how and when), names its trade-off (time, feeling awkward), and judges after the case week whether it changed how the people around responded. Step up from grade 8: from thanks for one costly help to a habit of thanks planned and checked.

words: norm; unwritten rule; fair; change plan
notes: Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student applies the fairness questions to an invented school norm (seniors-only tables in the commons) and to a settled case the courts have ruled on, then designs a plan to change the school norm through school channels, with its trade-offs, and judges which part would work best. Step up from grade 8: from naming what a change cost to designing a change plan. Teacher note: settled facts the courts have ruled on, taught with dignity; current political disputes are not SEL content.

cross_subject: health:g9-phw-factors-and-behavior (health on how factors at many levels shape behavior)
notes: Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student traces how an invented video app's feed and an invented school rule each push students' behavior, designs one change to either, and judges the change by who it would help and what it would cost. Step up from grade 8: from naming a system's pressure to redesigning a part of it. Teacher note: invented apps, accounts and posts only, never the student's own; no product names.

words: open question; assumption; source; change of mind
cross_subject: ela:e9-ri-argument-evaluate (judging whether reasoning holds and evidence is relevant)
notes: Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. Before deciding on an invented school-wide issue (a new phone rule), the student plans the questions to ask, the sources to check and what would change their mind, then judges after the case whether the questions found what mattered. Step up from grade 8: from staying open under friends' pressure to planning an open inquiry.

cross_subject: math:alg1-data-displays (comparing distributions with plots before a choice)
notes: Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student checks an invented claim spreading at school ("most students sleep six hours") against a class data set shown in two plots, plans a decision on what the data back, names what the data cannot show, and judges the decision with the look-back step. Step up from grade 8: from weighing evidence under time pressure to a data check designed and judged.

words: short term; long term; trade-off; review
notes: Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student lays out the short- and long-term results of options in an invented case (posting a clip of a class mishap that would get views), plans the choice with its trade-off, and later judges it against how the story unfolds. Step up from grade 8: from judging a costly choice afterward to planning ahead with a review built in.

Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student runs the six-step stop-think-choose on an invented choice pushed by a trending post, then compares it with the same choice made on a shortcut, and writes where careful thinking changed the result. Step up from grade 8: from thinking against a clock to judging a whole process against a shortcut.

Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student maps everyone an invented school decision reaches (a club's choice to post photos of an event), plans an option that weighs the far side too, and judges the plan against a stakeholder the map first missed. Step up from grade 8: from weighing who is affected against popularity to a designed option checked for gaps.

Unit 5, Norms, media and influence. The student plans a week for an invented student pulled between late gaming streams, sleep and a team counting on them, weighs well-being for self and others, and judges the plan's balance after the case week. Step up from grade 8: from one choice against something wanted to a balanced week planned and checked.

cross_subject: health:g9-phw-goal-assess-write (health applies a goal process to a health goal)
notes: Unit 6, Goals with others. The student designs a term goal with a partner on the goal steps card: milestones, what each partner does, the trade-off they accept and a midpoint check, then judges and revises the plan after an invented setback. The goal is checked at the unit's end and carried on as the unit's carry-out cue. Step up from grade 8: from monitoring one term goal to designing a shared one with its review.

words: initiative; start-up plan; recruit; first step
notes: Unit 6, Goals with others. The student designs a start-up plan for something a ninth-grade class lacks (a study group, a welcome table): who to ask, the first step, what could stop it and what it costs, then judges the plan after the first invented week. Step up from grade 8: from starting despite a cost to designing the start.

Unit 6, Goals with others. The class plans a proposal to improve one part of ninth-grade school life and the student designs their part on the goal steps card (the audience, the route, the evidence, the trade-offs), carries it out where the school allows and judges what worked. Student voice in class and school life, with no cause picked by the course. Step up from grade 8: from carrying out one part to designing it.

cross_subject: health:g9-meh-teams-negotiate-views (health on teamwork and negotiation in many settings)
notes: Unit 6, Goals with others. The team designs its own plan for a shared project (roles, norms, how to raise a problem), carries it out, and holds a short look-back at the end to judge what to keep and change. Step up from grade 8: from carrying a project under a deadline to designing and judging the team's way of working.

Unit 6, Goals with others. The student plans how to lead a team session (an agenda, how the group will decide, how to hear every voice), runs it, follows when another member leads, and judges both roles from team feedback. Step up from grade 8: from leading one unpopular decision to planning and judging a whole session.

words: upstander plan; safe option; support; report
notes: Unit 6, Goals with others. The student designs an upstander plan for an invented case of a student left out of a team in a hurtful way: the safest option, the words with the I-statement frame, support for the person afterward and when to report, rehearses the words with a partner while the teacher or a card plays the unkind act, then judges the plan against the case. Step up from grade 8: from planning one costly speak-up to a plan with follow-up. Teacher note: no student plays the unkind part or the one treated unfairly; school life only, and no cause is chosen by the course.

Unit 6, Goals with others. On an invented team split over a project choice, the student writes the other side's view well enough that its holder would agree, plans a question to check it, and judges whether the summary held up when the case gives more. Step up from grade 8: from taking one costly view to planning how to test that one has it right.

cross_subject: physical-education:g9-encourage-feedback (encouraging others and giving feedback)
notes: Unit 6, Goals with others. The student plans how a team leader could credit each member's work across a project (what to notice, when to say it), and judges after the case which credit landed and why. Step up from grade 8: from crediting a rival once to planning credit across a team.

words: listen to understand; paraphrase; both sides; check back
cross_subject: ela:e10-sl-seminar (the same student-led discussion norms)
notes: Unit 1, Listening to understand. With a partner, the student plans a talk on an invented disagreement where each person thinks the other is not listening, rehearses it with both people using the check-back step, and judges from the partner's account whether each felt understood. Grade 10 brings the other person's side of the talk into the plan.

words: viewpoint; reason; strongest case; common ground
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-contested-questions (naming where informed people agree and disagree)
notes: Unit 1, Listening to understand. The student writes the strongest form of two invented classmates' opposed views on a school question, plans a conversation that finds common ground, and judges whether each person would accept how they were described. New this year: two people's views held at full strength.

Unit 1, Listening to understand. In an invented scene the student reads one person's feelings, then reads the same moment through the second person's eyes, plans a response for each, and judges which reading the case bears out. This year the scene is read from both sides.

Unit 1, Listening to understand. The student maps the think-feel-do loops of two invented people in one misunderstanding, with what each cares about shown in the loop, plans where either could break the loop, and judges which break the case supports. Grade 10 runs the loop for a second person beside the first. Teacher note: a thinking skill used on characters, not a treatment; no student is asked to test their own thoughts aloud.

Unit 1, Listening to understand. The student traces how an invented school system (a points reward for attendance) looks to a student it helps and to one it pushes out, designs a change, and judges it from both views. A second person's view now tests the redesign. Teacher note: invented apps, accounts and posts only, never the student's own; no product names.

Unit 2, Hard conversations. With a partner the student plans and holds an invented hard conversation over a shared commitment, each writing the other's interests before the talk, then agrees a fix with the I-statement frame and checks it later. Grade 10: each side plans from the other's interests. The teacher plays any upset part.

Unit 2, Hard conversations. The student plans how to offer help to an invented friend who may not want it, writes how the offer could sound from the friend's side, uses the support map to plan when an adult must come in, rehearses the offer with a partner playing the friend, and judges the plan after the scene. New in grade 10: help planned around the other person's wishes. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor. A worry about a friend's safety goes to an adult, even when the friend asked for a secret. Crisis topics are health's (health row g9-meh-suicide-and-self-harm-help).

Unit 2, Hard conversations. The student designs a plan for keeping a strong feeling from driving an invented hard talk, adds how the other person's feeling might rise too and what the plan does about it, and judges it in a rehearsed scene. What grade 10 adds: two people's feelings in one plan.

words: cool down; shared pause; signal; return
notes: Unit 2, Hard conversations. The student builds a coping plan for two people in an invented tense talk: an agreed pause signal, a tool each could use, and how to come back to the talk. The student rehearses it with a partner and judges whether the pause helped both. New this year: the coping plan works for two people at once. Teacher note: breathing, stretching and pausing as plain body skills, with no spiritual framing. Stress and mental health topics are health's (health rows g9-meh-influences-judge-plan and g9-meh-suicide-and-self-harm-help), named in the teacher notes. Teacher note: if a student tells of harm or risk, follow health's steps (docs/courses/health/APPROACH.md, "If a student tells you something"): the school's reporting route and the counselor.

words: own feeling; other's feeling; name aloud; pattern
notes: Unit 2, Hard conversations. The student charts the feelings of both people in an invented hard conversation, finds where they set each other off, and plans where naming a feeling aloud could slow the talk, judging the chart against the scene. Grade 10 charts a second person beside the first. Teacher note: checks name a character's feeling and its clue; no clinical words; a student's own feeling is never recorded.

Unit 2, Hard conversations. The student plans how to raise a class concern with a teacher or school leader (an invented crowded test schedule), writes how the adult may see it, revises the plan to answer that view, and judges the talk after a rehearsal. The other person's view now shapes how voice is used. Student voice in class and school life, with no cause picked by the course.

Unit 3, Culture and respect. Main year for working across difference in 9 to 12. In an invented mixed team, the student plans working norms with a partner from another background, each writing how the other sees a clash (eye contact, directness, time), and judges the norms after a scene. Grade 10 builds the norms from both people's sides. Teacher note: no student is asked to explain their own culture; customs come from stories and invented partners.

cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-apartheid (an unfair system and how it was resisted, taught in world history this year)
notes: Unit 3, Culture and respect. Main year for unfair norms in 9 to 12. The student applies the fairness questions to a settled case (school segregation, struck down by the Supreme Court in 1954, or apartheid as world history teaches it), writes how the norm looked to the people it held down and to those who kept it, and plans a fair change to an invented school norm. New this year: the norm seen through the eyes of the people it hurt. Teacher note: settled history, taught with dignity: school segregation was struck down by the Supreme Court in 1954; apartheid's laws were repealed from 1990 to 1991 and it ended with the 1994 election; current political disputes are not SEL content. The history itself is social studies' (wh2-apartheid).

Unit 3, Culture and respect. The student writes how an invented character sees their own groups and how a newcomer sees them, plans how the character could make room for the newcomer while staying themselves, and judges the plan after a scene. Grade 10 sets one person's sense of self beside how another sees them. Teacher note: invented character first; a student may make up their own; family and culture are never asked about by name in a check.

Unit 3, Culture and respect. The student plans how an invented team could use a member's strength from a home language or culture (translating for a visitor, a family tradition of storytelling), writes how the member might want it used or not, and judges the plan from that member's side. This year the strength holder's own wishes shape the plan. Teacher note: home languages and culture are welcome when offered, never asked about.

Unit 3, Culture and respect. Main year for snap judgments in 9 to 12. The student plans how an invented student could check a snap judgment about a classmate from another school, writes how the judged classmate would experience the guess, and judges whether the plan corrected it. What grade 10 adds: the judged person's view. Teacher note: invented cases only; the skill is noticing and checking one's own guesses, never blame of a group.

Unit 3, Culture and respect. The student plans credit for an invented teammate whose strength others overlook because it looks different from theirs, writes how the teammate would hear it, and judges the words. The teammate's view now decides whether credit lands.

Unit 3, Culture and respect. Privately the student plans how to weigh an interest against what another person expects of them (a friend, a coach), writes that person's view fairly, and judges after a set time whether the choice kept their own purpose. Grade 10 brings another person's expectations into the plan. Teacher note: the list stays with the student; it is checked only that the steps were followed, never for its content.

Unit 4, Saying no, setting limits. The student plans how an invented student could set a limit in a friendship (a friend who wants every free period together), writes how the friend may hear it, plans the talk with the I-statement frame and its check-back, rehearses it with a partner playing the friend, and judges the plan from both sides after the scene. Grade 10 weighs the friend's side of the limit. The limits are about time, help and plans. Teacher note: no real friends are named; dating and relationship health topics are health's (health rows g9-v-abuse-and-dating-violence and g9-sh-health-and-consent, with consent and boundaries in health row g9-meh-boundaries-consent).

words: refusal; limit; alternative; keep the friend
cross_subject: health:g9-meh-boundaries-consent (health practices stating limits in friendships, work and online)
notes: Unit 4, Saying no, setting limits. The student designs a refusal for an invented case where a friend presses them to lie to a teacher for the friend, writes how the friend sees the ask, plans an alternative that keeps the friendship, rehearses against a card character and judges what held. notes: Unit 4, Communities and systems. Owner year for 9 to 12. Unit 4, Communities and systems. Owner year for 9 to 12. Grade 12 says no at work.
